title: The Valley of Dry Bones and the Two Sticks
summary: The Spirit sets Ezekiel in a valley full of very dry bones and God asks whether they can live. At the prophet's word the bones come together and are covered with flesh, and when he prophesies to the breath they stand up alive, a vast army. God explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, hopeless in exile, and that he will open their graves and bring them home. In a sign-act, two sticks labeled Judah and Joseph become one, picturing a reunited nation under one king, David, with God's sanctuary among them forever.
story: Chapter 36 promised a new heart and God's Spirit within his people. Chapter 37 shows what that means, in a vision the exiles could not forget. Their own words had become a proverb of despair: our bones are dried up, our hope has perished. God answers not with an argument but with a picture of death reversed. The second half of the chapter takes up an older wound. Israel had been divided into two kingdoms since the death of Solomon, and the northern kingdom had been lost for more than a century. The restoration God promises heals that division too. The chapter's closing promise of God's sanctuary among his people forever points forward to the temple vision of chapters 40 to 48, after the battle with Gog in chapters 38 and 39.
historical:
The vision is undated, but it belongs to the period after Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC, when the exiles' hope had collapsed (verse 11). The division of the kingdom goes back to about 930 BC, when the ten northern tribes rejected Solomon's son Rehoboam and made Jeroboam king (1 Kings 12). The northern kingdom, often called Israel, Ephraim, or Joseph after its leading tribe, fell to Assyria in 722 BC and its people were deported. Judah, the southern kingdom, had now gone into exile as well.

So when Ezekiel speaks of "the whole house of Israel" (verse 11) and joins the stick of Joseph to the stick of Judah, he is promising more than the return of the recent exiles. He is promising the reconstitution of all twelve tribes as one people, a hope that the prophets kept alive (Jeremiah 3:18; Hosea 1:11) long after the north had disappeared as a political entity.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, to lie unburied was one of the worst fates imaginable. Bodies left on a battlefield for birds and beasts were a mark of defeat and curse (Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 7:33). The bones in this valley are the slain (verse 9), a defeated army left to bleach in the sun, and they are very dry, meaning long dead and beyond any natural hope. For a priest like Ezekiel, bones and corpses were also the strongest source of ritual impurity (Numbers 19:11-16), which makes his being led all around among them more striking.

The sign-act of the two sticks uses a practice familiar from ancient record-keeping, writing names or ownership marks on wooden rods or tablets. Numbers 17 records Moses writing the name of each tribe on a staff. The joining of the sticks may have been done so they looked like one in the prophet's hand. The vision later became one of the most beloved images in Jewish art and memory; the third-century AD synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria, for example, has a wall painting of it.
literary: The chapter has two parts: a vision report (verses 1 to 14) and a sign-act with its interpretation (verses 15 to 28). The vision unfolds in two stages. At the first prophecy the bones assemble and are covered, but "there was no breath in them" (verse 8); only at the second, addressed to the breath, do they live. This two-stage creation deliberately recalls Genesis 2:7, where God forms the man from dust and then breathes life into him. The Hebrew word ruach carries the chapter, meaning spirit (verse 1), breath (verses 5 to 10), winds (verse 9), and God's Spirit (verse 14). The interpretation quotes the people's lament and answers each phrase. The second half builds from the image of one stick to a cluster of promises, each marked by forever or everlasting: land, king, covenant, and sanctuary.

outline.t: The valley of very dry bones: can these bones live?
The first prophecy: bones, tendons, flesh, skin
The second prophecy: breath and a vast army
The meaning: graves opened, Spirit given, home again
David their prince and God's sanctuary forever

doctrines.note: "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live" (verse 14). The Spirit is God's life-giving power, the same breath that animated the first human. The chapter joins the gift of the Spirit to the gift of life itself.

The people say "our hope has perished; we are cut off" (verse 11), and God answers that he will open their graves. Hope in this chapter doesn't depend on any sign of life in the bones; it rests on God's word and power.

The two sticks become one in God's hand (verse 19). The division of God's people is not permanent in his purpose; the restored people are one nation under one shepherd, a promise the New Testament applies to Jew and Gentile made one in Christ.

The chapter ends with an everlasting covenant of peace and the covenant formula: "I will be their God, and they will be My people" (verse 27). The goal of restoration is God dwelling among his people.

words.note: Ruach, breath. The same word means wind and spirit, and the chapter moves between the senses on purpose: the breath that enters the bodies comes from the four winds (verse 9) and is finally identified as God's own Spirit (verse 14). Life, in the Bible's view, is always God's breath.

Etsem, bone. Ten times in the chapter. Bones were the last remains of the dead, and dry bones were the image of total, long-settled death. The people apply the word to themselves: our bones are dried up.
Qever, grave. In the interpretation the valley becomes a graveyard, and God promises to open the graves of his people. The image of exile as death and return as resurrection is here made explicit.
Miqdash, sanctuary, holy place. The chapter's final promise is God's sanctuary among his people forever (verses 26 and 28), which leads into the temple vision of chapters 40 to 48.

christ: The New Testament hears this chapter in several places. After his resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22), an act that echoes both Genesis 2:7 and this vision of breath giving life. Jesus spoke of the hour when the dead in the tombs would hear his voice and come out (John 5:25-29), language close to God's promise to open the graves. He called himself the one shepherd of one flock (John 10:16), and John says he died to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:52). Paul quotes God's promise to dwell among his people and be their God (2 Corinthians 6:16), words found here in verse 27 and in Leviticus 26:12, and applies them to the church as God's temple. Revelation 21:3 announces the final fulfillment: God's dwelling is with humanity. The vision is first about the nation's revival, but Christians have rightly seen in it the pattern of the gospel: life given to the dead by the Spirit through the word.

hard.q: Is this chapter about the resurrection of the dead or only about Israel's return from exile?
hard.a: In its own setting the vision is explained as a picture of the nation's revival: the bones are the whole house of Israel, their graves are the exile, and their resurrection is the return to the land (verses 11 to 14). Most scholars therefore read it primarily as a metaphor for national restoration, and note that the fuller Old Testament hope of individual bodily resurrection appears more explicitly later, in Daniel 12:2. Yet the metaphor only works because resurrection was imaginable as something God could do, and later Jewish and Christian readers took the image to point to the literal resurrection as well; rabbinic discussion in the Talmud debated whether the dead Ezekiel saw were actually raised. Many Christian interpreters read the chapter on two levels: it promises the restoration of God's people, and it anticipates the bodily resurrection that the New Testament grounds in Christ's own rising. Both readings agree that only God's word and Spirit can give life to what is dead.

questions: When God asks "can these bones come to life?" Ezekiel answers "only You know." What situations in your life or community feel like a valley of dry bones?
The bones were assembled before they were alive (verse 8). What is the difference between a community that has the right structure and one that has God's breath?
The two sticks become one in God's hand. Where do you see division among God's people, and what would it take to see it healed?
